reviews.text: as a mediocre chess player and rather bad than good puzzle solver, i can absolutely recommend this game. great and interesting interface design and a creative approach to expanding the game of chess. the daily chess puzzles and the leaderboard are very fun and motivating and regularly make my head spin :D

So far so good, got a chance to play tonight. You power up your pieces, solve chess puzzles, and it scratches that chess itch and the turn-based style games that Im a fan of. The daily challenge leaderboard might become a problem for me — I’ve already sent it to my friends so we can compete. Funny moment: I got caught at a wedding playing chess.com on my phone while waiting for the ceremony. The guy next to me told me to put my phone away, then whispered to me he was working on a chess game. I told him I was excited for a new chess game coming out and showed him some of the links I sent my friends about "Below the Crown"… turns out it was that was the game he was work on. Small world! Good content for Early Access.

Do you like chess? Buy this game Do you like sneaky puzzles and think on your feet tactical turn based combat? Buy this game. Do you like good games? Buy this.. you get the picture. Please note: I didn't say "Are you good at chess?". That doesn't matter. The game has a lot of features so you can focus on the tactics and traps, instead of "Wait which piece goes where" and "Am I in danger?" As there's literally a sixth sense button that shows all tiles currently in danger of being able to be attacked. Chess is a lot more fun when you can quick glance the board and focus more on where to toss a freeze spell or an exploding knight.

Let us ponder for a moment, how tragic life would be if you are someone who likes games, indie games, and board games, and you did not immediately smash "buy" when you saw Tim Keenan came out with another game. There's no knowing the bounds of misery you must be in, while you are disastrously spending $10 on anything OTHER than this game. Your mother would be ashamed of you and your dog: embarrassed to be seen in public by your side. WHAT A QUICK REMEDY AWAITS! It should come as no surprise that this game is fantastic. About a decade ago, at an Illuminati meeting of indie game devs at an undisclosed location (you think that part is a joke too, but it's not), we played Chess The Gathering prototypes in person and the devs of all genders stroked their proverbial goatees and said "there's definitely something here". Now, playing the game, it's clear that it came together as hoped: layers of deck-building, roguelike, dungeon-crawling, RPG mechanics upon the timeless, indefatigable mechanics of chess piece movement. Why are you still reading? Shed your indolence, add this game to your collection, and bask in a creation that was built by one of the most brilliant game development minds in the world, over a period longer than the construction of a skyscraper! GO PLAY!! :D

At first I bought it because it was from the same creator as Duskers, and it turns out it's a good twist on the typical chess gameplay.

Bite-sized chess with per-run upgrades and debuffs, over-game progression, varied boards (rooms), and a mechanism to keep games brief. I play chess-likes, but not really played chess since I was a kid. I imagine AI could probably be better - quite slow when toggled to enhanced and then becomes difficult to outmanoeuvre by brute force, but careful use of piece deployment, upgrades and powers stack the deck in your favour. One of the better mini chess-likes I've played, and the kind of pacing and challenge that can be addictive.

When I first played this it had a crash bug on Linux (that also caused entire system crash, apparently just eating all the memory) - good news, a few weeks later, the issue seems to be gone. So now that that's fixed, the game is a lot of fun. The visual kind of cyberpunk style is pleasant. The weird interjections of questions about your mental health are interesting. Nothing to complain about audio-wise. Gameplay-wise I appreciate that it's *not too chess*, while still being *enough* chess that things are familiar and don't need a lot of explanation. I recently played "The Rookery" which is also decent, but one thing I found frustrating there was the requirement to complete a checkmate in a number of moves, which makes it so you still have to "seriously chess" sometimes. As a lazy video gamer I prefer not to have to seriously chess, so Below the Crown fits my preference much better, in that there's no time limit after which you lose (the board shrinks so if you're having a hard time closing it out, taking longer actually helps), and it doesn't even require you to organize a checkmate, you also win if you just capture every other piece. There's also levels with different win conditions, which I appreciate as an enjoyer of variety. The Rookery has a similar "drop new pieces" model, but the difference here of doing it via your wizard-piece's line of sight (vs Rookery is just drop anywhere) gives it just enough extra trickiness to make dropping pieces still feel like part of the tactics. One cruel thing about Below the Crown, which is maybe a down-point versus Rookery, is there is a [limited] undo button, but even if you have spare uses, you can't use it to undo a really bad mistake where the result is your wizard gets captured. So you have to pay extra attention to those sneaky bishops all the way across the board. Anyway, in summary, this game is fun for a person who's okay at chess but doesn't really want to play chess, and is probably also fun for a person who's good at chess but doesn't take it too seriously. I doubt it would be fun for someone who *hates* chess. Edit after playing it some more - there's less story-escalation than I expected, which is a shame. It's more of a "just do the same thing again but with an added difficulty factor," with nothing really new unlocking. e.g. I expected some sort of special boss for unlocking and playing "act 3", but it was just the same knight-king boss level as I've had before in act 2. Would still recommend, but less than I thought.

A refreshing chess roguelike with fair pieces, fun concepts, and phenomenal presentation. A lot of problems I have with other chesslikes is that the pieces can be super overpowered, and hard to play around. In this game, there isn't any queen that also moves like a knight that can check you into eternity on move one. Instead, the pieces are all normal for the exception of a couple of interesting variants that really only place restrictions on their original counterparts, which leads to some very thought provoking situations. The positions are also very fair. Coupled with the obstacles and obstructions and the fact that you start without any of your pieces and have to move the wizard (effectively the king) before placing a piece or casting a spell forces you to really think far ahead from move one, instead of just building up an overpowered board and slamming into the enemy until you mate them. The presentation is also amazing, the retro feel with the vibrant neons and scanlines, the constant buzz of archaic electronics, and the overall feel of the dungeons being reminiscent of 80s and 90s retrotech kinda reminding me of some Tron kind of feel, all of it culminates for a great late night vibe with a whiskey in hand, feeling like MacReady in The Thing. On top of that is the cool themes of the questionnaires and the looming mystery of the emperor break the flow of your constant calculations in the best way possible. Abruptly pulling you into a different long line of questions and theories. Only gripe I have are no draw arrows like in the online chess games but I'm sure this will be coming at some point. An interesting game. Built on the scaffolding of chess but with rules and objectives altered enough to require a new way of thinking about the pieces and how to utilize them. Queens have a handicap knocking them down to being about equal in value with rooks and bishops. Kings can move into check as long as the game will be won by doing so. The board is always changing in shape and layout. The pieces can have special abilities drastically changing their effectiveness. Overall it is a fun and worthwhile experience. There is some room for improvement to the interface ( special abilities don't have unique icons on the pieces requiring a hover to see what they do - and often these drastically change how they should be used ) and a couple inconsistencies in pieces that add for confusion. ( like the queen losing her handicap but only when she is your chosen king ) But what I found was that all of these changes in behavior and rules provides a challenging strategy game where you will find yourself thinking carefully on what your best move/action combo is going to be at every turn. Sometimes the choices are obvious and the round is simplistic. Other times it takes careful thought the whole way through. But it will seldom be a situation of doing the same thing you did last time.
